What is a Wrongful Death Claim?
The definition of wrongful death in Colorado is a death caused by the neglect, default or wrongful act of another person. Wrongful death cases are
civil actions

and are not part of the criminal justice system. Success in a wrongful death claim rests on the type and amount of evidence presented by the family filing the claim. The wrongful death case process may involve several phases, such as:
Mediations
Demands
Settlement
Jury trial

A Denver wrongful death attorney can guide your family through all of the phases of a civil claim, negotiating for a fair resolution on your behalf. Proving a wrongful death claim requires the family’s attorney to prove four legal elements:
Negligence.
The death occurred as a result of the careless or reckless actions of another. Negligence in personal injury law is carelessness that causes an injury or death to another person.
Breach of duty.

The responsible party owed the deceased a duty of care. A duty of care is a legal obligation to act responsibly and in a manner that a reasonable and prudent person would in the same circumstances. A breach of duty is any violation of this requirement.
Causation.

The negligent party breached this duty of care, and this breach caused the resulting wrongful death. Unlike in a criminal case, you do not need to prove the defendant intended to take the life of your loved one. Instead, you simply must show that the defendant’s negligence caused the fatal injury.
Damages.
Actual damages resulted, such as pain and suffering, added medical costs, loss of earnings, income, inheritance, or guidance.

As the plaintiff in a wrongful death lawsuit, you must establish these elements as more likely to be true than not true. This is called a preponderance of the evidence. A Denver wrongful death lawyer can help your family members gather clear and convincing evidence to establish these elements and obtain a fair settlement award for your substantial losses.

Common Causes of Wrongful Death in Denver
Fatal incidents rarely happen the same way twice, but a
Denver wrongful death lawyer
tends to see the same categories surface again and again. Common causes we see across Denver include the following:
Motor Vehicle Accidents:

Speeding, impaired driving, and distracted driving remain leading factors in fatal crashes along high-volume corridors like I-25 and I-70, where dense traffic and frequent lane changes can increase collision severity
Commercial Trucking Accidents:
Fatal collisions involving semi-trucks and delivery vehicles often involve multiple potentially liable parties, from the driver to the trucking company to a cargo loader
Premises Liability Incidents:
Fatal falls, inadequate security, and hazardous property conditions may support a wrongful death claim against a property owner or manager who failed to maintain safe conditions
Motorcycle Accidents:
Motorcyclists may face disproportionate risk at Denver intersections, where visibility and right-of-way violations can play a central role in fatal crashes
Drunk and Impaired Driving:
Impaired drivers were connected to roughly a third of Colorado’s traffic deaths in the most recent reporting year, a pattern reflected on Denver’s own roadways

No matter the cause, the key legal question remains the same: Did negligence, recklessness, or a failure to act reasonably lead to the death of a loved one? A wrongful death claim answers that question through the civil court system, which works differently from a criminal case.
Wrongful Death vs. Criminal Case

Understanding these categories matters because a wrongful death claim and a criminal case are not the same thing, even when they arise from the same incident. Wrongful death is a civil tort, not a crime. A civilly liable party pays the surviving beneficiaries financial damages, while a criminal conviction for murder, homicide, or vehicular manslaughter results in a sentence against the defendant.
A few key differences separate the two in Denver:
Intent:

Criminal cases require proof that the defendant knowingly and intentionally committed the crime. A wrongful death claim carries no such requirement. You can hold someone responsible even if their careless, unintentional, or unwitting conduct puts your loved one in danger.
Burden of Proof:

A criminal conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt, while a wrongful death claim only requires a preponderance of the evidence, roughly a 51 percent likelihood. This gap exists because a conviction can result in imprisonment, whereas a civil claim results only in monetary damages.
Your Role:

A prosecutor, not your family, decides whether to bring charges and carries the burden of proving them. You may be asked to give a statement or testimony, but your involvement is far more limited than in a civil lawsuit you help direct.

If the responsible party also faces criminal charges, Colorado courts may pause your statute of limitations until that case concludes, giving your family more time to file. A conviction does not automatically establish civil liability, since the two cases apply different standards, but it can serve as evidence supporting your claim.
Who Can File a Wrongful Death Lawsuit in Colorado?

body.alt: Banner saying, "am I eligible to file a wrongful death claim?" in Colorado

children.text: A
Denver wrongful death lawyer
can help determine who has the right to file a wrongful death lawsuit, since Colorado law restricts this right to certain surviving loved ones under
. The rules change depending on how much time has passed since the decedent’s death:
A surviving spouse may file within the first year
A surviving spouse or children may file in the second year, or parents if there is no spouse or child
A personal representative of the estate may file at any time

Other family members, such as siblings, nieces, nephews, and grandparents, generally do not have the right to file wrongful death claims in Colorado. If the decedent had other beneficiaries financially dependent on them at death, they may be entitled to a share of any settlement. At
Dormer Harpring
our team can help answer any questions about who is eligible to file.
Wrongful Death Claim Process in Colorado
Once it is clear who has the right to file, the next question is what happens after that decision. A Colorado wrongful death claim generally moves through several stages before reaching resolution:
Investigation:
Our attorneys review police reports, medical records, and available evidence to help determine liability before a claim is filed
Notice and Filing:
A formal claim is filed with the appropriate Denver-area court, and the defendant receives notice of the pending action
Negotiation:
Most wrongful death claims are resolved through settlement discussions or mediation rather than trial
Litigation:
When a fair settlement cannot be reached, the case may proceed to trial, where a judge or jury determines the outcome
Each stage carries its own deadlines and evidentiary demands, and missing one can affect the outcome of an otherwise strong claim.

How to File a Wrongful Death Claim in Colorado
Filing the claim involves several concrete steps, each with its own requirements under Colorado law:
An attorney should be consulted promptly, since speaking with a
Denver wrongful death lawyer
early can give the legal team more time to prepare a strong case.
An attorney can draft and file the complaint with the appropriate civil court in the county where the incident occurred or where the defendant resides.
The defendant must receive formal notice, as Colorado law requires proper service of the lawsuit before the case can proceed.
Once served, the defendant has a set period to respond, which can determine how quickly the case proceeds to its next stage.
Our team can help families move through each of these steps without missing a critical deadline.
What Evidence Can Be Used to Prove Wrongful Death?

Proving the grounds for a wrongful death claim generally falls to the family and their attorney, and the evidence gathered should be compelling enough to support the family’s account of events. Key evidence that may support a claim includes the following:
A copy of the police or accident report
Video surveillance footage and photographs of the scene of the accident
The decedent’s medical records
A coroner’s report
Accounts that eyewitnesses gave of the fatal accident
A criminal conviction against a defendant for intentionally or wantonly killing a loved one
Cell phone records
Accident reconstruction
Wrongful death expert testimony
Our team can file letters of preservation or request subpoenas to help secure this evidence early, then work to present a clear picture for a judge or jury.
How Long Do I Have to File a Wrongful Death Claim in Colorado?
In Colorado, a wrongful death claim must generally be filed within two years from the date of death, under

. Certain exceptions can pause or extend this deadline in specific situations, such as when the deceased was a minor or when the responsible party also faces criminal charges for the same death, but these exceptions are not the rule. Families should not assume an exception applies without confirming it with a
Denver wrongful death lawyer
. Missing this deadline typically means losing the right to pursue compensation entirely, which is why prompt legal guidance matters from the earliest point after a loss.
How Much is a Wrongful Death Case Worth in Colorado?

A wrongful death case in Colorado can involve economic damages, non-economic damages, and in certain cases, punitive damages. The specific value of any individual case can depend heavily on the circumstances involved, including the deceased’s income, age, and the strength of the evidence supporting the claim. While economic damages have no statutory cap in Colorado, non-economic damages are capped at $2,125,000 as of January 1, 2025, under
, a significant increase from the previous cap of roughly $679,990.
Compensation for Wrongful Death Claims

Damages in a wrongful death claim can help compensate a family for the pain and suffering their loved one experienced before death, as well as repay the family for monetary expenditures and non-monetary losses that followed. Examples of wrongful death damages include:
Medical expenses incurred before the loved one’s death
Funeral and burial expenses
Loss of the financial support and services the deceased would have provided
Loss of an expected inheritance
Loss of consortium, including companionship, guidance, and emotional support

In cases involving especially reckless or intentional conduct, punitive damages may also be available. The value of a wrongful death claim can depend on the circumstances involved, including the loved one’s income level and the amount of insurance available to cover the family’s losses. No dollar amount can ever match the value of a loved one’s life, but a compensatory award may help a family manage expenses and achieve greater financial stability during a difficult time.

faqs.question: What Happens if the Deceased Has No Surviving Immediate Family Members?

children.text: The estate of the deceased may file a “survival action” to make up for expenses like burial and medical costs if there are no surviving parents, spouses, or children, and as of 2025, siblings.

faqs.question: Can a Wrongful Death Lawsuit Impact a Life Insurance Policy?

children.text: No, wrongful death lawsuits have no effect on life insurance payouts. They are not affected by legal claims for wrongful death damages.

faqs.question: Can I File a Wrongful Death Claim if the Death Occurred at Work?

children.text: Yes, but unless a third party—someone other than the employer—is held legally liable for the death, the claim might only be eligible for workers’ compensation benefits.

faqs.question: What Kind of Evidence Can Strengthen a Wrongful Death Case?

children.text: Your wrongful death claim may be strengthened by witness statements, accident reports, medical records, expert testimony, and financial documentation of losses.

faqs.question: Can I Still File a Wrongful Death Claim if the Victim Was Partially at Fault?

children.text: Yes. According to Colorado’s comparative negligence law, you can get compensation if the deceased person was less than 50% at-fault. However, the awarded damages will be decreased based on the percentage at-fault.

faqs.question: What’s the Difference Between Negligence and Manslaughter in Wrongful Death Cases?

children.text: A failure to use caution which results in an unintentional death is considered negligence. A criminal charge involving careless or intentional behavior is considered manslaughter. Wrongful death cases are made up of civil lawsuits based on negligence instead of criminal guilt.

faqs.question: What if Multiple Family Members Want to File a Wrongful Death Claim?

children.text: Colorado law sets specific requirements on who is able to file a wrongful death claim and when. Only the surviving spouse can file a claim during the first year after death. Children or other heirs can file a claim separately or jointly after a year.
